overview.text: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it crosses between materials where it travels at different speeds; light is a familiar example. At an angled boundary, a speed change makes the ray turn, while the direction of bending depends on whether it slows or speeds up. For light, the refractive index n = c/v compares its speed in a vacuum with its speed in a material, and Snell’s law (n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂) predicts the angles, measured from the perpendicular (normal) to the boundary. Refraction explains why a pencil partly submerged in water can look bent and enables lenses in eyeglasses and telescopes to redirect light.

key_facts.text: The refractive index of a material is the speed of light in a vacuum divided by its speed in that material: n = c/v.
For light entering a slower medium at an angle, the ray bends toward the perpendicular; entering a faster medium bends it away.
Snell’s law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, relates the indices of refraction to the ray’s angles in each medium; those angles are measured from the perpendicular to the boundary.
Different refractive indices in air and water make a pencil partly submerged in water appear discontinuous or bent.
Refraction is used by lenses in eyeglasses and refracting telescopes to redirect light.
